why does my voice sound weird on recordi.topic: Why does my voice sound weird on recordings?

scenes.subtitle: Have you ever recorded your own voice and wondered, "Is that really what I sound like to everyone else?" It's a common mystery.
When you speak, you hear your own voice through two pathways: air vibrations and vibrations through your skull bones.
Bone conduction makes your voice sound deeper and richer to you because it transmits lower frequencies more efficiently.
Recordings only capture the sound waves traveling through the air, exactly as others hear your voice externally.
This absence of bone-conducted frequencies on a recording makes your voice sound higher-pitched and less full to your own ears.
So, your recorded voice is actually how everyone else hears you! Give this video a like and follow for more interesting facts!

does your brain actually create its own.topic: Does your brain actually create its own sense of time?

scenes.subtitle: The clock on the wall doesn't dictate your sense of time. Your brain actively constructs its very own, unique perception of how moments unfold.
It's all thanks to specialized neural networks and brain regions that act like internal 'pacemakers.' They don't just count seconds, but interpret experiences.
When your attention is focused or emotions are strong, your brain processes more information. This 'data density' makes time feel like it's rushing by.
When bored or waiting, your brain receives less new information. This 'data flow' reduction makes your internal clock stretch, making moments feel incredibly slow.
Your memories also influence time. Novel experiences create more distinct memories, making a past period feel longer when you look back on it.
Yes, your brain absolutely sculpts its own subjective sense of time. To make life feel longer, embrace new experiences! Follow for more fascinating insights!
